title: What to prepare before a website redesign
summary: A practical preparation checklist for leaders who need to turn a website project into a clear business decision rather than a rushed visual exercise.

children.text: A redesign is easier to direct when the business questions are answered before visual exploration begins. The goal is not to write a perfect brief; it is to give the project enough commercial and operational context to make good decisions early.
Bring the business context into the room
Name the audiences the site must serve and the questions each audience needs answered before taking action.
Map the services, offers, locations, or capabilities that need a clear place in the information architecture.
Collect the proof that can be published: approved outcomes, credentials, project examples, team expertise, and client permissions.
Identify the systems the website must connect to, including CMS ownership, forms, analytics, booking, locations, or customer workflows.
Define the decision process: the people who approve scope, content, design, release readiness, and launch timing.
Use the preparation work to reduce ambiguity

A website can only represent what the team has decided to communicate. When audiences, proof, content ownership, and approvals are unresolved, the project carries those decisions into design and engineering. Addressing them first creates a more useful brief and a more dependable route to launch.
A useful first question
Ask: what must be clearer, easier, or more trustworthy for the people we most need to serve? The answer becomes a better foundation than a request to make the site look more modern.

title: How to evaluate website performance beyond a speed score
summary: A framework for reading performance evidence in context, separating diagnostic lab tests from the experience of real visitors.

children.text: A score can reveal useful issues, but it is not a verdict on a website. Performance is about whether people can access and use the important parts of a page under the conditions they actually encounter.
Separate diagnostics from lived experience

Lab tools simulate a controlled visit and are useful for finding problems to investigate. Field data reflects observed visits, where device capability, network quality, geography, and content variation can change the outcome. Both sources are useful, but they answer different questions.
Check the page and user journey being measured, not only a site-wide average.
Record the measurement source, device profile, test conditions, and collection timeframe before comparing results.
Look for the page element and delivery dependency behind a metric, then verify that a proposed change helps the intended visitor experience.
Treat third-party scripts, media, fonts, and content changes as operational inputs that need ongoing review.
Use Core Web Vitals as evidence, not marketing shorthand

Largest Contentful Paint is one measure of perceived loading progress: it marks when the page's main content has likely loaded. It is valuable because it points toward a meaningful moment in a visit, not because it can be reduced to a generic promise.
For technical teams, the
web.dev guidance on LCP
and its discussion of field debugging are useful starting points for connecting measurement to diagnosis.

title: What a controlled website launch should include
summary: A launch-readiness framework that treats release as a coordinated operational change, not a final design handoff.

children.text: A website launch changes more than a URL. It affects discoverability, customer paths, content ownership, analytics, integrations, and the team responsible for responding once the site is live.
Define release readiness before the launch window
Confirm the approved scope, content, assets, destinations, and person responsible for final go/no-go decisions.
Test key paths with realistic inputs: navigation, forms, booking or commerce flows, analytics events, error states, and contact routes.
Review accessibility with both automated checks and intentional manual testing, including keyboard behavior and content structure.
Prepare redirects, DNS, monitoring, rollback responsibility, and the editorial handoff before the release begins.
Keep the first release period observable

The launch window should include an agreed way to observe errors, form delivery, indexing signals, and the critical paths visitors use. This does not guarantee a business outcome; it confirms that the team can verify the release and respond to issues from a known baseline.
The
W3C accessibility evaluation guidance
is a useful reference for understanding why evaluation needs a deliberate method rather than a single automated scan.
